problem.title: Design a Write-Optimized LSM-Tree Storage Engine
problem.prompt: Design a RocksDB/LevelDB-style embedded key-value engine sustaining 250,000 random 1 KB writes/sec (250 MB/s) on NVMe SSD (3.5 GB/s seq write, 80K random read IOPS, 16 GB RAM cap) with <= 8 ms p99 point-lookup latency across 10 TB (90% negative lookups), < 10 s WAL crash recovery, and bounded compaction debt.

spark.summary: A B+Tree saturates 80K NVMe IOPS flushing random 16 KB dirty pages under 250,000 random writes/sec; an LSM-Tree converts writes into sequential appends.
spark.keyTakeaway: Append writes to a CRC32C-checksummed WAL + 64 MB SkipList MemTable, flush to L0 SSTables with 10-bit/key Bloom filters + sparse indexes, and run leveled compaction (L0->Ln) with L0 write-stall backpressure.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** At `250,000` random `1 KB` writes/sec (`250 MB/s`), a B+Tree must read `16 KB` leaf pages from disk, dirty them in RAM, and flush random `16 KB` pages back to NVMe—quickly saturating `80,000` random read/write IOPS and accelerating SSD garbage collection.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Group-Commit WAL + 64MB SkipList MemTable -> Immutable L0 SSTables (Put/Delete(k, v) -> CRC32C WAL (128MB) -> SkipList MemTable -> L0..Ln SSTables); MemTable -> Overlapping L0 -> Disjoint L1..Ln with Bloom Filters (MemTable (64MB) -> L0 SSTables (<=12) -> L1..Ln (10x ratio) -> 4KB Block).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS) incurs `2x` temporary space amplification (`20 TB` on a `10 TB` dataset) and poor point-lookup latency. Meet all write, read, RAM (`16 GB`), and recovery (`< 10 s`) targets: **Write & Crash Path**: Group-commit to a `CRC32C`-checksummed WAL (`32 KB` blocks; truncate at first.

**Failure Modes & Application:** LSM-Trees power the storage layer of modern distributed databases: **RocksDB / Pebble**: Embedded inside CockroachDB, TiKV, Kafka Streams, and Spark Structured Streaming state stores.

An **LSM-Tree** turns every `Put` and `Delete` into sequential appends.

learningJourney.title: 90% negative lookup amplification, L0 write stalls, and torn WAL records
learningJourney.explanation:
Naive LSM-Tree implementations fail on three fronts:

1. **90% Negative Lookup Read Amplification**: Without Bloom filters, checking whether a missing key exists forces disk reads across every L0 SSTable and L1..Ln level, blowing past the `8 ms` p99 SLA.
2. **L0 Write Stalls**: If foreground writes (`4` flushes/sec of `64 MB` MemTables) outpace `L0 -> L1` compaction, overlapping L0 files pile up and freeze writers.
3. **Torn WAL Tail on Crash**: Unclean power loss leaves a partial WAL record that halts recovery.

learningJourney.title: Naive size-tiered compaction and unindexed SSTables
learningJourney.explanation: Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS) incurs `2x` temporary space amplification (`20 TB` on a `10 TB` dataset) and poor point-lookup latency. Meanwhile, scanning SSTables without per-SSTable `10-bit/key` Bloom filters wastes 90% of NVMe IOPS on negative lookups.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise solution: Leveled Compaction + Bloom Filters + Tombstone Scoring
learningJourney.explanation:
Meet all write, read, RAM (`16 GB`), and recovery (`< 10 s`) targets:

- **Write & Crash Path**: Group-commit to a `CRC32C`-checksummed WAL (`32 KB` blocks; truncate at first checksum mismatch on crash -> `128 MB` replays in `< 0.5 s` at `3.5 GB/s`). Insert `(userKey ASC, seqNum DESC)` into a `64 MB` SkipList MemTable (flushes every `0.256 s`).
- **Read Path (`<= 8 ms` p99)**: Check Active MemTable -> Immutable MemTables -> L0 SSTables -> at most 1 SSTable per `L1..Ln` (10x level multiplier). `10-bit/key` Bloom filters (`~1%` false positive) eliminate 99% of negative disk seeks within the `16 GB` RAM budget.
- **Compaction & Guardrails**: Soft throttle at `12` L0 files, hard stop at `24`, parallel subcompactions, and priority compaction of SSTables with `> 20%` tombstones + range-delete tombstones.

sectionDiagram.summary: Disjoint L1..Ln key ranges and 10-bit/key Bloom filters bound point lookups to <= 8 ms even at 10 TB.

learningJourney.title: Where LSM-Tree storage engines are used
learningJourney.explanation:
LSM-Trees power the storage layer of modern distributed databases:

- **RocksDB / Pebble**: Embedded inside CockroachDB, TiKV, Kafka Streams, and Spark Structured Streaming state stores.
- **Cassandra / ScyllaDB**: Uses MemTable + SSTable + leveled/time-window compaction for high-ingest wide-column workloads.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

knowledgeCheck.question: In an LSM-Tree handling 90% negative lookups across 10 TB, how do 10-bit/key Bloom filters and Leveled Compaction keep p99 `Get()` under 8 ms?

options.text: Bloom filters reject ~99% of absent-key SSTable checks in RAM, and Leveled Compaction keeps L1..Ln key ranges disjoint so at most 1 SSTable per level is probed
options.feedback: Correct: Bloom filters eliminate disk reads on negative lookups, and disjoint L1..Ln ranges bound worst-case read amplification.

options.text: Bloom filters store all 10 TB of key-value payloads inside the 16 GB RAM block cache
options.feedback: Bloom filters only store compact bitsets (~10 bits per key) to test set membership, not full values.

options.text: Leveled Compaction disables the Write-Ahead Log so writes never touch NVMe
options.feedback: The CRC32C WAL is always written sequentially for crash durability.

options.explanation: Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always observes its own completed writes.
The write was durable on the primary; the replica simply lagged.
Atomicity governs all-or-nothing commit, not cross-replica visibility.

_problemQuestions.prompt: Why does placing `request_timestamp` at the very beginning of a 3,000-token system prompt hurt latency and cost?

options.explanation: BPE still tokenizes the text normally.

options.text: It invalidates prefix/KV caching for all subsequent 3,000 tokens on every request
options.explanation: Correct! Prefix KV caching requires an exact token match from index 0 onward.
Output length is unaffected; Prefill cache reuse is what breaks.
